author: reek
body: Two properties decide whether that shape is usable, and neither is settled by the render test that motivated it. The mark is bound in a pure let ABOVE an effectful bind, so the question is whether it is taken before the effect runs. And the value the bind produced has to be read AFTER the restore, so the question is whether an Integer survives a restore that rewinds the allocator past the point where it was produced.

author: reek
body: The plain arm is the control on the instrument. If it does not grow, the loop is not allocating and the bracketed arm's flatness says nothing.

author: reek
body: Something has to be allocated inside the iteration or there is nothing for the bracket to reclaim. A four-element list is the cheapest thing that is definitely heap.

author: reek
body: The third arm is the one that decides whether the placement matters at all. It brackets exactly the same work with the mark BELOW the bind, so whatever the effect itself allocates escapes. Against an effect that allocates nothing the two placements agree and this arm reads flat; the arm earns its place by being able to disagree.

author: reek
body: An effect that allocates nothing cannot express the difference between the two placements, and the pair above duly agrees. So the last pair uses an effect that DOES allocate before it answers, which is what a real device poll does when its idle path builds anything at all. These two run the same work and differ only in which side of the bind the mark sits, and they are the reason the placement is a decision rather than a preference.

author: reek
body: The above arm is run twice at different counts on purpose. Its first call reads a few hundred bytes, and taken alone that looks like a small residual leak; a second call at twice the iterations reads ZERO, which says the first figure was a one-time cost of entering the path and not a per-iteration one. One measurement could not have told those apart and would have been quoted as the wrong thing.
